questions.a: Enterprises that combine inputs also create chances for people to take part in economic activities

questions.a: I-B, II-D, III-A, IV-C
o: I-B, II-D, III-A, IV-C

questions.q: What does the chapter mean by a business or enterprise? Give one example of an enterprise that provides a service rather than a good.
questions.a: A business or enterprise is a firm, a shop, a factory, etc., which produces or sells goods or provides a service. Example of a service enterprise: a salon (haircut and grooming) or a mobile repair shop.
s: Defines an enterprise as a firm, shop or factory that produces or sells goods or provides a service
Gives one service enterprise, such as a salon or a mobile repair shop

questions.q: Answer in short. (a) What does the word 'land' cover in economics besides geographical land? (b) Name any four natural resources that the chapter includes under land. (c) State the two ways in which a business can get the land it needs.
questions.a: (a) It also covers natural resources. (b) Any four of soil, forests, water, air, sunlight, minerals, oil and natural gas. (c) A business either purchases the land or pays rent to use it for a period of time.
s: (a) Land also means natural resources
(b) Any four of soil, forests, water, air, sunlight, minerals, oil, natural gas
(c) Purchase the land, or pay rent to use it for a period of time

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A shop that pays rent for its plot, instead of buying it, does not use land as a factor of production.
Reason (R): Businesses either purchase the required land or pay rent to use it for a period of time.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Renting is one of the two ways a business gets land, so the shop still uses land as a factor of production.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
A small dairy near Anand keeps its cows on a rented field and uses water from a well. It owns a milking machine and a delivery van and employs four workers. Its owner, Hetal, put her savings into the dairy and decides how it is run. Answer each part in one line.
(a) Name the four types into which economics classifies the factors of production.
(b) Which factor are the rented field and the well water?
(c) Which factor are the milking machine and the van?
(d) Which factor is the effort of the four workers?
(e) The chapter does not count technology as one of the four types. What role does it give technology?
questions.a: (a) Land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. (b) Land, because land in economics includes natural resources such as water, and a business may pay rent to use land. (c) Capital, as they are human-made durable assets used in production. (d) Labour, the physical and mental effort used in production. (e) Technology is a facilitator that enables an enterprise to produce more goods with the same or fewer inputs.
s: (a) Land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship
(b) Land, as land includes natural resources such as water and may be rented
(c) Capital, as human-made durable assets
(d) Labour, physical and mental effort
(e) Technology is a facilitator: more goods with the same or fewer inputs

Labour
Productivity

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes human capital as the chapter uses the term?
questions.a: The specialised skills, knowledge, abilities and expertise needed to perform labour
o: The specialised skills, knowledge, abilities and expertise needed to perform labour

The money and machines that a business uses to produce goods

questions.q: True or false: In the chapter, 'labour' means only the physical effort of people who work with their hands. Give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: False. Labour is the physical and mental effort used in production. Carpenters, farmers, construction workers, teachers and doctors all supply labour, using physical strength, knowledge and skill in different amounts.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: labour is physical and mental effort, so teachers and doctors also supply labour

questions.q: Nasreen and Pooja both work eight hours a day at a mobile repair shop. Nasreen has finished a six-month course in repairing phones; Pooja joined last week and has had no training. (a) Which factor of production do both of them supply? (b) Which of them brings more human capital to the shop, and what does that change about her work, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) Both supply labour, the physical and mental effort used in production. (b) Nasreen, because her training has given her specialised skills and knowledge. Human capital is the quality and efficiency of labour, not just its basic effort, so her eight hours give better and more efficient work.
s: (a) Both supply labour (physical and mental effort)
(b) Nasreen: training gives specialised skill, which raises the quality and efficiency of her labour

questions.q: A furniture firm in Saharanpur employs a carpenter who carves table legs and a software developer who handles its online orders. The owner says only the carpenter is a 'resource' in production, because only he makes the furniture. Which statement, based on the chapter, shows that the owner is wrong?
questions.a: Both are a resource, because each applies knowledge, skills and decision-making to create goods and services
o: Both are a resource, because each applies knowledge, skills and decision-making to create goods and services
The developer is capital rather than labour, because his work is done on a computer
Both are a resource only because the firm pays each of them a salary
Both are a resource only because each has finished a training course for the job

questions.q: Lalitha joined an optician's shop in Mysuru to fit lenses into spectacle frames (the figures are illustrative). In her first week she fitted 4 frames a day, of which 3 had to be redone. After six weeks of daily practice and a short training course, she fits 10 frames a day and none has to be redone. (a) Using the chapter's definition, has Lalitha gained a skill? Name the two things that built it. (b) Work out how many correctly fitted frames she turned out a day in week 1 and in week 6. (c) The shop gets an order for 45 frames to be ready in 5 working days, and Lalitha must do it alone. Show whether she could have met it in week 1 and whether she can meet it now, and say what this shows about her human capital.
questions.a: (a) Yes. A skill is the ability to do an activity or job well with practice and training; her daily practice and the training course built it. (b) Week 1: 4 - 3 = 1 correctly fitted frame a day; week 6: 10 correctly fitted frames a day. (c) In week 1 she could fit only 1 x 5 = 5 frames, far short of 45; now she can fit 10 x 5 = 50 frames, enough for the order. Her human capital (specialised skill and knowledge) has grown, and human capital covers the quality and efficiency of labour, not just its basic effort.
s: (a) Yes: skill is doing a job well with practice and training; daily practice and the course built it
(b) Week 1: 1 correct frame a day; week 6: 10 a day
(c) Week 1: 5 frames, short of 45; now 50 frames, enough; her human capital (quality and efficiency of labour) has grown

questions.q: A speaker at a school meeting says, 'By 2023, India's adult literacy rates for men and women had become almost equal.' Using the chapter's World Bank figures for 2023, (a) work out how many in every 100 men and how many in every 100 women aged 15 and above could not read and write with understanding a short, simple statement about their everyday life, and (b) say whether the speaker is right.
questions.a: (a) Men: 100 - 85 = 15 in every 100; women: 100 - 70 = 30 in every 100. (b) The speaker is wrong: the male rate (85 per cent) is 15 percentage points above the female rate (70 per cent), and in every 100 adults, twice as many women as men cannot read and write.
s: (a) Men 15 in every 100; women 30 in every 100
(b) Wrong: 85 against 70 per cent, a 15-point gap; twice as many women as men cannot read and write

questions.q: Answer in short. (a) What is a demographic dividend? (b) According to the Economic Survey of India 2024, what share of people in India are below the age of 35? (c) Name any two things that individuals must have access to if India is to take advantage of this young population.

(b) 65 per cent
(c) Any two of quality education, health, training, skilling

questions.q: True or false: Meghna is 13 years old and can read and write a short, simple statement about her everyday life with understanding, yet she is not counted in India's adult literacy rate. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. The adult literacy rate counts only people aged 15 and above, so a 13-year-old is not part of it, however well she reads and writes.
s: States the verdict: True
Reason: the adult literacy rate covers only people aged 15 and above

questions.q:
A district (the figures are illustrative) can fund only one programme this year.
Programme P: evening classes in reading and writing for 3,000 adults who cannot read.
Programme Q: a one-year machine-repair course for 1,000 young people who can already read and write.
Programme R: a primary health centre for a block where children miss on average 30 school days a year through illness.
(a) Name the facilitator of human capital that each programme builds.
(b) Using the chapter, explain how Programme R would help the children learn.
(c) Using the chapter, explain how Programme P could raise the productivity of the adults.
(d) Link the three programmes to the chapter's condition for India to reap a demographic dividend.
(e) Recommend one programme for this district, justify it with the data, and say what the district gives up.
questions.a: (a) P and Q both build the facilitator 'education and training' (P basic literacy, Q training for a particular job; naming 'education and training' for both is accepted), and R builds healthcare. (b) Good health supports cognitive development, the process of learning, knowing and understanding, so children attend school regularly and learn better instead of missing 30 days a year. (c) Literacy helps enhance the skills and productivity of human capital, so adults who can read can do more in a particular time period. (d) The chapter says India can benefit from its young population only if individuals have access to quality education, health, training and skilling; each programme supplies one of these. (e) Any choice justified from the data that names what is given up: for example R, because 30 lost school days a year hold back the learning of every child in the block, giving up literacy for 3,000 adults; or Q, because 1,000 literate young people are ready for job skills now, giving up the health centre.
s: (a) P and Q: education and training (P literacy, Q job training); R: healthcare
(b) Good health supports cognitive development, so children attend regularly and learn better
(c) Literacy raises skills and productivity: more done in a given time
(d) Demographic dividend needs access to education, health, training and skilling
(e) A recommendation justified with the data that names what is given up

questions.a: The shilpa shastras are ancient texts that contain detailed design guidelines on sculptures, paintings, buildings, wooden items and jewellery. Texts on sculpture prescribe exact specifications for any two of postures, colours, measurements and proportions of figures.

questions.q:
A maritime museum in Kochi has built a full-size model of an ancient Indian ship. Its label says only: 'Model of a ship of a kind that Indians built for over 2000 years. Not a single nail was used anywhere in its hull. Ships like this made long voyages from India's coasts.' A Class 8 group visiting the museum has been asked to write a fuller label.
(a) If no nails were used, how were the wooden planks of the hull joined?
(b) Why did this method help the ships at sea?
(c) Across which ocean did these ships sail, and for what two purposes?
(d) What happened to this technique after the 16th century, and for what is it still used?
questions.a: (a) The wooden planks were stitched together using cords. (b) Stitching made the ships flexible, which helped them navigate the ocean with ease. (c) The Indian Ocean, for maritime trade and cultural exchanges. (d) It saw a severe decline after the Europeans arrived in the Indian Ocean in the 16th century; it is now used for making small fishing boats.
s: (a) Planks stitched together with cords
(b) Stitching made the ships flexible, so they navigated with ease
(c) Indian Ocean; maritime trade and cultural exchanges
(d) Severe decline after the Europeans arrived; now used for small fishing boats

questions.q: The chapter calls the tools of ancient Indian craftspeople 'a type of technology'. (a) Using the chapter's meaning of technology, explain why a sculptor's chisel can be called technology. (b) What did craftspeople do with their tools that shows how they saw their work, and under what names does this tradition continue? (c) A classmate says the chisel is old technology that must by now have been replaced. Using the chapter, explain why that does not follow.
questions.a: (a) Technology means the application of scientific knowledge, and any production-related activity uses some form of technology; the chisel is such a form, used to make sculptures. (b) They worshipped their tools, as work was an offering done with devotion; the tradition continues as Vishwakarma puja or Ayudha puja. (c) The chapter says some early forms of technology from ancient times are still in use today, and progress does not always mean replacing old technology, as pulleys and wheelbarrows show.
s: (a) Technology is applied scientific knowledge and every production activity uses some form of it
(b) Tools were worshipped; continues as Vishwakarma puja or Ayudha puja
(c) Early forms of technology are still in use; progress does not always replace old technology

questions.q: Arjun wants to open a single tea stall at a bus stand. He says, 'I will raise the money by selling shares on the stock market, like big companies do.' Using the chapter, (a) state the source of funds that people generally turn to first when they start a business, (b) state what Arjun could do if that is not enough, and (c) explain why the stock market route that the chapter describes does not fit his tea stall.
questions.a: (a) Personal savings, family and friends. (b) Take a loan from a bank to meet the shortfall, paying interest along with a part of the loan amount over a period of time. (c) The chapter describes the stock market as the way large companies that need a lot of money to expand raise it from the general public, offering a share of the profits (a dividend); a single new tea stall is not such a company.
s: (a) Personal savings, family and friends
(b) A bank loan for the shortfall, repaid with interest over time
(c) The stock market is how large companies needing a lot of money to expand raise it; a single tea stall is not one

questions.q:
Farhan has run an e-rickshaw repair workshop in Lucknow for three years (the figures are illustrative). He works with spanners, a battery tester, a small van and a rented plot. He started it with Rs 2 lakh of his own savings and Rs 1 lakh from his brother. Now he wants to open a second workshop that will cost Rs 6 lakh, and he has Rs 2.5 lakh saved. Offer 1: a bank will lend him the whole amount he is short of, to be repaid as Rs 4.2 lakh in all over three years. Offer 2: his brother lends him Rs 1.5 lakh without interest, and the bank lends only the rest, to be repaid as Rs 2.4 lakh in all over three years.
(a) Name two items in his workshop that are capital, and say why.
(b) How does the chapter describe the source of his starting money?
(c) How much must he borrow in all to open the second workshop?
(d) Work out the interest he would pay the bank under each offer, and decide which offer he should take, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Any two of the spanners, the battery tester and the van: they are human-made durable assets used to produce a service (the rented plot is land, not capital). (b) Personal savings, family and friends, which the chapter says are generally the first source of funds. (c) Rs 6 lakh - Rs 2.5 lakh = Rs 3.5 lakh. (d) Offer 1: Rs 4.2 lakh - Rs 3.5 lakh = Rs 0.7 lakh interest. Offer 2: the bank lends Rs 3.5 lakh - Rs 1.5 lakh = Rs 2 lakh, so interest is Rs 2.4 lakh - Rs 2 lakh = Rs 0.4 lakh. He should take Offer 2: it saves Rs 0.3 lakh of interest, because interest is paid only on what he borrows from the bank; this matches the chapter, where family and friends come first and a bank loan meets only the shortfall.
s: (a) Two of spanners, tester, van, as human-made durable assets used in production
(b) Personal savings, family and friends: the first source of funds
(c) Rs 3.5 lakh
(d) Interest Rs 0.7 lakh against Rs 0.4 lakh; Offer 2 saves Rs 0.3 lakh, family first and the bank only for the shortfall

questions.q:
Three friends in Guwahati start a venture that makes drinking straws from bamboo (the figures are illustrative). They pool Rs 1.5 lakh, rent a small plot of land, hire four local craftspeople, sell only through their own online store, and aim to sell in 10 cities within two years.
(a) Using three features of the chapter's definition, show that this venture is a startup.
(b) Which factor of production is the rented plot, and which factor do the four craftspeople supply?
(c) Name two tasks of an entrepreneur that the friends have performed, giving the evidence for each.
(d) State two ways, according to the chapter, in which such a venture can benefit society.
(e) One friend wants to close the online store to save money and sell only through one local shop. Evaluate this idea, using the chapter's definition of a startup.
questions.a: (a) It has limited resources (Rs 1.5 lakh), it aims at rapid growth and expansion (10 cities in two years), and it leverages technology (its online store). (b) The rented plot is land (rented for a period of time); the craftspeople supply labour. (c) Any two with evidence: combines factors of production (plot, craftspeople, money); takes risks by investing money and time (the pooled Rs 1.5 lakh); makes key decisions (selling only online). (d) It brings an innovative product to the market that benefits society, and it creates job opportunities and supports livelihoods (the four craftspeople). (e) A justified judgement: closing the store saves money from limited resources, but the venture would stop leveraging technology and would find it hard to grow rapidly to 10 cities, so the idea works against what makes it a startup.
s: (a) Limited resources, aim of rapid growth, leveraging technology, each tied to the data
(b) Plot is land; craftspeople supply labour
(c) Two tasks of an entrepreneur with evidence
(d) Innovative product for society; jobs and livelihoods
(e) Judgement weighing saving money against leveraging technology for rapid growth

questions.q:
A shirt unit in Tiruppur (the figures are illustrative) has 10 tailors working on hand-operated sewing machines, and together they stitch 200 shirts a day. A buyer offers a regular order that needs 320 shirts a day. The owner has two plans. Plan A: replace the 10 hand machines with electric machines; the same 10 tailors would then stitch 350 shirts a day. Plan B: keep the hand machines and hire 5 more tailors who work at the same speed as the present ones.
(a) Using the chapter's meaning of technology, show that the hand-operated machines are also technology.
(b) Work out how many shirts a day the unit would stitch under Plan B.
(c) Which plan meets the order? Show the comparison and give your decision.
(d) Which role of technology, described in the chapter, does Plan A show?
questions.a: (a) Technology means the application of scientific knowledge, and any production-related activity uses some form of technology; the hand-operated machine is an earlier form of technology that is still in use. (b) Each tailor stitches 200 / 10 = 20 shirts a day, so 15 tailors stitch 15 x 20 = 300 shirts a day. (c) Plan A gives 350 shirts, which meets 320; Plan B gives 300, which falls 20 short. So Plan A should be chosen. (d) Technology as a facilitator that enables an enterprise to produce more goods with the same or fewer inputs: the same 10 tailors stitch 350 shirts instead of 200.
s: (a) Technology is applied scientific knowledge; the hand machine is an earlier form still in use
(b) 20 shirts per tailor, so 15 tailors stitch 300 a day
(c) Plan A 350 meets 320; Plan B 300 is 20 short; choose Plan A
(d) Facilitator: more goods with the same or fewer inputs

questions.q:

(b) Acquire raw materials, assemble and install software, test phone

questions.q:
Consider these statements about how the factors of production are connected.
I. When a farm starts using more machines, the proportion of factors it uses can change.
II. If one factor is missing or misused, production can become inefficient or be halted.
III. Relying on far-off sources instead of local inputs can halt production if the supply chain is disrupted.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III
o: I, II and III
I and II only
II and III only
I and III only

questions.q: A bakery in Shillong (the figures are illustrative) has 3 ovens. Each oven bakes 100 loaves a day, but only when one baker runs it, and the bakery has only 2 bakers. Which statement fits the chapter's account of how the factors of production are connected?
questions.a: It bakes at most 200 loaves a day and one oven stands idle: the factors complement each other, so a shortage of one makes production inefficient
o: It bakes at most 200 loaves a day and one oven stands idle: the factors complement each other, so a shortage of one makes production inefficient
It bakes 300 loaves a day, because the extra oven makes up for the missing baker
It bakes no loaves at all, because production halts whenever any one factor is short
It bakes 300 loaves a day, because baking is capital-intensive and needs little labour

questions.q:
A cold-pressed coconut oil unit in Kozhikode (the figures are illustrative) stands on a rented plot, runs two oil presses bought with a bank loan, employs 12 workers and is run by its founder, Anitha, who took the risk of starting it. It buys coconuts from nearby farms, but its bottles come from one supplier 2,000 km away who offers many designs. Last month a transport breakdown held up the bottles for 10 days, and the unit could not send out any oil.
(a) Classify the rented plot, the oil presses, the 12 workers and Anitha under the four factors of production.
(b) Using the chapter, explain why the unit could not send out oil though it had coconuts, presses and workers.
(c) What does the chapter call the network that brings the bottles to the unit, and what risk does it link with relying on far-off sources?
(d) State the advantage the chapter gives for procuring inputs from different geographic locations.
(e) Next month Anitha can deal with only one of two problems: (i) one of her two presses will be out for repair for 10 days, or (ii) her bottles will again arrive 10 days late. Each press produces enough oil to fill 150 bottles a day. Work out how many bottles of oil the unit could send out over those 10 days if she deals only with (i), and if she deals only with (ii), and decide which problem she should deal with, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Rented plot: land; oil presses: capital; 12 workers: labour; Anitha: entrepreneurship. (b) The factors complement each other and are interconnected; when one input is missing, production can become inefficient or be halted, so without bottles the oil could not be sent out. (c) The supply chain; relying on far-off sources instead of local inputs means a disruption can halt production. (d) Geographic interconnectedness gives businesses access to varied inputs. (e) If she deals only with (i), the bottles are still late, so the unit sends out 0 bottles: production halts. If she deals only with (ii), one press still runs: 150 x 10 = 1,500 bottles, so production is only inefficient. She should deal with (ii), the bottles: without bottles nothing can be sent out and production halts, while with one press down production only becomes inefficient. The chapter says the factors complement each other, and a missing factor can make production inefficient or halt it.
s: (a) Plot land, presses capital, workers labour, Anitha entrepreneurship
(b) Factors complement each other; a missing input halts production
(c) Supply chain; far-off sources risk a halt when disrupted
(d) Access to varied inputs
(e) Only (i): 0 bottles (halt); only (ii): 1,500 bottles (inefficient); deal with the bottles

questions.q: True or false: According to the chapter, using natural resources responsibly means that producers should stop using natural resources altogether. Give the reason or the correct statement.
questions.a: False. Producers do use natural resources such as land, water and minerals; using them responsibly means meeting our needs today without making it harder for future generations to meet theirs, by reducing waste, avoiding pollution and adopting sustainable practices that replenish natural resources.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: use resources so today's needs are met without harming future generations, by reducing waste, avoiding pollution and sustainable practices

questions.q:
A leather-finishing unit near Vellore in Tamil Nadu employs 150 local workers (the figures are illustrative). It releases 50,000 litres of wastewater a day into a nearby river, and farmers downstream complain that the water has harmed their fields. The owner now plans a plant that will clean and reuse 40,000 litres of this wastewater every day and release only the rest into the river.
(a) According to the chapter, how do such factories help the local economy, and what harm can their waste do?
(b) How many litres a day would still go into the river, and what fraction of the earlier amount is this?
(c) Which practice shown in the chapter does the owner's plan follow, and why does the chapter want producers to adopt such practices?
(d) The owner says that once the plant runs, the unit will have met every responsibility the chapter names. Using the chapter, explain why this is not yet enough for its 150 workers.
questions.a: (a) Many people earn money by working in leather factories, which helps the local economy, but their waste can pollute rivers and soil. (b) 50,000 - 40,000 = 10,000 litres a day, which is one-fifth of the earlier amount. (c) Recycling industrial wastewater before releasing it into water bodies, a sustainable practice; producers should adopt sustainable practices to replenish natural resources for future use, so that needs today are met without making it harder for future generations to meet theirs. (d) The chapter also names responsibilities towards workers: fair compensation and a safe working environment; investing in skill development and training; and following laws on workplace rights such as fair treatment, no discrimination and benefits like health care or paid leave. The plant meets none of these.
s: (a) Gives people work and helps the local economy; waste can pollute rivers and soil
(b) 10,000 litres a day, one-fifth of the earlier amount
(c) Recycling wastewater before release; sustainable practices replenish resources for future generations
(d) Responsibilities to workers: fair pay and safety, skill training, workplace rights

questions.q: Under India's CSR law, a cement company in Rajasthan must spend Rs 60 lakh on CSR activities this year (the figures are illustrative). Its manager proposes: (i) Rs 25 lakh to fit filters that cut the dust its kilns release into the air; (ii) Rs 20 lakh for a drinking-water plant in the village next to the factory; (iii) Rs 30 lakh to open a new sales office in another city. (a) Which of the three proposals fit the chapter's description of CSR, and which part of the description does each match? (b) How much of the Rs 60 lakh do these proposals cover, and how much is still to be planned? (c) The manager argues that the sales office should also count because it will create jobs. Judge this, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) (i) fits 'reducing polluting activities' and (ii) fits 'addressing the well-being of local communities'; (iii) does not fit. (b) Rs 25 lakh + Rs 20 lakh = Rs 45 lakh, so Rs 60 lakh - Rs 45 lakh = Rs 15 lakh is still to be planned. (c) The argument does not hold: CSR is about addressing social and environmental concerns in a business's operations to benefit society and biodiversity, such as cutting pollution or caring for local communities, while a sales office serves the company's own growth in sales, even if it creates some jobs.
s: (a) (i) reducing polluting activities, (ii) well-being of local communities; (iii) not CSR
(b) Rs 45 lakh covered; Rs 15 lakh still to plan
(c) Not valid: CSR addresses social and environmental concerns for society; a sales office serves the company's own growth
